learn.title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
learn.headline: Claude Code settings files can leak your secrets when pushed to GitHub
learn.reason: Approvals you click get saved in a file; keep that file out of Git.

card.headline: Claude Code settings files are leaking passwords onto public GitHub
card.gist: Claude Code remembers commands you approve in a file, often with any passwords inside. Researchers found thousands of these files posted publicly on GitHub.
card.picture: It's like an ETL job log that prints the full database connection string. On your laptop, that is mostly harmless. Commit that log to a public repo, and anyone can read the password.
card.why_you: You use Claude Code every day. Before you push a project, check that this settings file is not included.
card.remember: Approved commands can hold passwords. Check files before you push.
card.term_meaning: A password or key written directly into a command or file, instead of kept separately.
card.say_it: I keep secrets in environment variables, not inside commands, because tools may save commands to files.
card.follow_up_why: Because tools like Claude Code may store approved commands in files that can get committed.
card.reality_check: Security researchers at Apiiro found this. Anthropic's docs say the file is usually ignored by git.
card.try_it: In a project folder, run: git check-ignore -v .claude/settings.local.json. Then open that file and look for passwords.

learn.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 enforce the prefix check for every account, whatever its age.
learn.headline: Claude Fable 5.2 rejects requests that edit earlier conversation messages.
learn.reason: Agent loops that edit old messages now fail; check your code first.

card.headline: Claude's newest models reject chats whose earlier parts were edited
card.gist: On Anthropic's newest Claude models, your code must not edit earlier parts of a chat. If it does and resends the model's earlier reasoning, the request fails.
card.picture: Think of an append-only audit table. New rows always go at the bottom. Edit an old row, and every later row fails its check.
card.why_you: When you build chat apps or agents, keep earlier messages fixed and only add new ones. Code that rewrites history will start failing on these models.
card.remember: Only add to the end of a chat. Never edit earlier parts.
card.term_meaning: The API checks that the system prompt, tools, and earlier messages match what was sent before.
card.say_it: I keep the system prompt and tools fixed, and only append messages, so saved reasoning stays valid.
card.follow_up_why: Because each reasoning block is tied to everything sent before it, so editing that history invalidates it.
card.reality_check: This comes from Anthropic's own API docs. The docs suggest test requests set to error on any edit.
card.try_it: Open any chat script you have. Find every place that changes the system prompt or old messages between turns.

We’ve launched fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 in Messages API requests on the Claude API.

learn.title: Thinking Machines: Inkling 2 Small (free) is now callable (free in / free out per M tokens, 1048K context)
learn.headline: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small now free to call via OpenRouter.
learn.reason: Free access to a large reasoning model; useful for practicing API calls cheaply.

card.headline: A new reasoning model from Thinking Machines is free on OpenRouter
card.gist: A new model from Thinking Machines Lab is free to use through OpenRouter. Your prompts and answers are logged and used to improve their models.
card.picture: Think of a free public SQL sandbox. You run real queries at no cost, with a limit per minute. The owners keep your queries to improve their service.
card.why_you: You have no paid key, so this is a free way to test agent code. The free version is meant for agent tools, like coding assistants. Never send work data.
card.remember: Free models often pay with your data. Never send private work.
card.term_meaning: A model split into many expert parts, where only a few parts run for each token.
card.say_it: Inkling 2 Small is mixture-of-experts: 594B parameters total, but only 17B active per token.
card.follow_up_why: Because running only some experts per token lowers compute per answer, while keeping large total capacity.
card.reality_check: This is OpenRouter's own listing; scores come from Artificial Analysis. Free use is rate limited and logged.
card.try_it: Point an agent tool that supports OpenRouter at this model. Run one small task with no private data.

also.title: Meta: Muse Ember is now callable ($0.10 in / $0.50 out per M tokens, 1048K context)

learn.title: A 0.1B model just killed 8B embedding models... I tried it out.
learn.headline: Tiny 0.1B SPLADE model claims to beat large embedding models for search.
learn.reason: Shows how small local search models could fit RAG; the claim is unverified.

card.headline: A tiny search model beat a bigger one in one user's test
card.gist: A Reddit user replaced a heavier search model with a small keyword-style one that also understands meaning. In their own test, it found documents better using far less memory.
card.picture: It's like the index at the back of a textbook. Each page is listed under a few important words, so lookup is quick. This model builds that index, but understands what words mean.
card.why_you: You are learning RAG, where an AI answers using documents it searches first. This gives you a light search option to test on your Mac.
card.remember: For local search, test a small model before a big one.
card.term_meaning: Search that stores each text as a few weighted words, instead of a long list of numbers.
card.say_it: For local RAG, I'd compare sparse retrieval like SPLADE against dense embeddings on my own eval set.
card.follow_up_why: Because retrieval quality depends on your own data, so one person's result may not hold for mine.
card.reality_check: This is one Reddit user's test, on mostly Korean documents, promoting their own tool. The model is free to try.
card.try_it: Write ten questions about your own notes, each with its correct document. That is your first retrieval eval.
